title: Azure Australia East 2023: Voltage Sag, Chillers That Would Not Restart
dcName: Australia East Availability Zone datacenters, Sydney (not named)

severity.usersAffected: Customers in one Australia East zone across about 50 Azure services, plus Microsoft 365 and Power Platform; ARM errors worldwide for resource groups homed in the region; AKS in Australia Southeast.
severity.tier: Two data halls in one Availability Zone, with regional and global side effects

brief: On 30 August 2023 a lightning-induced voltage sag tripped chillers at an Azure Australia East zone. A control timing defect kept 13 from restarting; by the time staff reached the last five by hand their water was too hot. Two halls overheated and were shut down. Most VMs were back that night; full recovery took until 3 September.

magnitude.note: Two halls in one zone, but about 50 services and global ARM effects. Duration (8): about 4 d 9.5 h from first impact to full mitigation, inside the 3–7 d band; 99% of VMs recovered in about 12 hours.

rootCause:
TRIGGER: at 08:41 UTC on 30 August 2023 lightning struck electrical infrastructure about 18 miles from one Australia East Availability Zone in Sydney. The resulting voltage sag shut down cooling chillers across several datacenters.

COOLING CHAIN: 13 chillers did not restart automatically. Microsoft later traced this to a timing defect in the Chiller Management System, exposed because load growth in the zone had left the chillers in a susceptible operating configuration. The onsite team restarted chillers by hand on the rooftop, moving datacenter by datacenter in adjacent order. By the time they reached the last five, which served two adjacent data halls, the chilled-water loop was too hot and the chillers' self-protection refused to start. The two halls needed at least four chillers out of their seven.

IMPACT CHAIN: equipment began shutting down at 10:30; at 11:34 the team powered down the rest of the two halls to stop the thermal runaway, which let the loop cool and the chillers restart at 12:12. Recovery of storage, one SQL tenant ring and dependent services (Cosmos DB, AKS, ARM) stretched to 3 September.

LATENT ROOT: a control-timing defect that only showed under a voltage dip, a manual restart order that did not protect every hall, and platform services (ARM storage, an AKS queue database, a SQL gateway) not yet zone-redundant inside a region built on zones.
contributingFactors: A lightning-induced utility voltage sag shut down chillers across several datacenters (Azure PIR).
A timing defect in the Chiller Management System, exposed by load growth, stopped 13 chillers restarting automatically (Azure PIR).
Manual restarts followed an adjacent, building-by-building order; the last five chillers were reached after their loop water was too hot (Azure PIR).
Chiller self-protection blocks a restart when the chilled-water loop is too hot (Azure PIR).
Storage recovery was slowed by fault-detection resets, tooling performance and automation marking healthy nodes unhealthy (Azure PIR).
Some platform services were not zone-redundant: ARM storage, the AKS operation-queue database and one SQL gateway (Azure PIR).
One SQL Database tenant ring with 20 failed nodes had to be evacuated completely, extending recovery to 3 September (Azure PIR).
Cosmos DB failover waited 33 minutes to fail over its control plane, which was already zone-resilient (Azure PIR).

coe.action: Change control timing logic in the Chiller Management System so voltage dips do not block restarts
Change the emergency manual-restart order from 'adjacent' to hall 'load based' so every hall keeps partial cooling
Raise technician staffing at the site as an interim measure
Storage: optimise large-scale recovery data and troubleshooting guides
coe.status: Estimated completion December 2023 (completion not reported in the PIR)

coe.action: Service Fabric and SQL Database: more reliable tenant-ring recovery, auto-failover group criteria, mass migration tooling
Cosmos DB: faster Service Managed Failover for single-region-write accounts
AKS: make operation-queue databases zone-redundant and replace cross-region SQL queues with zone-redundant Service Bus
ARM: finish migration to zonally redundant storage
Incident management: harden readiness and playbooks for power-down scenarios
Remote shutdown of the remaining equipment in the two halls to stop the thermal runaway

lessonsLearnt: Chiller restart after a voltage dip is a control-logic problem as much as a mechanical one; test restart under real dip profiles as load grows.
Manual restart order matters: restore some cooling to every hall first, then finish each one.
Hot loop water locks chillers out; shedding IT load early can be the fastest way to get cooling back.
Zone redundancy only protects services that use it; internal platform dependencies must meet the same bar as customer guidance.
Recovery tooling and automation must work when many nodes come back at once and cannot report diagnostics.
Zone-redundant and multi-region configurations stayed available; locally redundant ones did not.
improvements: Cooling controls: chiller management timing fix (Microsoft, completed).
Procedure: load-based emergency restart sequence and interim extra staffing (Microsoft, completed).
Platform: zone-redundant AKS queues, ARM storage and SQL gateway (Microsoft, scheduled).
Recovery: storage, SQL and Cosmos DB recovery improvements (Microsoft, scheduled).
Analyst recommendation (not in the PIR): periodic sag tests of chiller restart at current load, and a chilled-water temperature alarm tied to an early IT load-shed decision.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Thirteen chillers and one timing defect
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The plant had spare chillers: seven for two halls that needed four. A control-timing defect, exposed by load growth, kept 13 chillers across the site from restarting after the sag, so the spare capacity existed but could not start.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Restart order decided which halls overheated
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The team went building by building. The last five chillers, serving two adjacent halls, were reached after their loop water had become too hot to restart. Microsoft found that a load-based order with the same staff would have prevented impact.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Shedding load to recover cooling
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The 11:34 decision to power down the two halls lowered the heat load, cooled the loop and let the chillers start 38 minutes later. It cost availability but ended the runaway.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Two halls, worldwide effects
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: ARM's storage for the region was not yet zone-redundant, so customers anywhere managing resource groups homed in Australia East saw errors, and AKS in Australia Southeast depended on a database in the failed zone.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: A four-day tail
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: 99% of VMs were back the same evening, but a few storage nodes needed hardware replacement and one SQL tenant ring had to be emptied, so full mitigation came on 3 September.

technicalDeepDive:
A chiller tripped by a voltage dip needs a restart; if the controller's timing logic misreads the dip, the restart never happens. Once the loop water warms beyond the chiller's safe entering temperature, the machine locks itself out to avoid damage, so every minute of delay makes the restart harder. Microsoft's fix was to the control timing, plus a new emergency restart order: restart by hall load so every hall keeps some cooling, instead of finishing one building before moving on.

The platform story is about zone redundancy. Zone-redundant storage, zone-redundant SQL and multi-region Cosmos DB stayed up. Locally redundant storage, a SQL gateway, the AKS operation-queue database and ARM's storage layer were not yet zone-redundant, so a failure of two halls in one zone reached customers in other zones and even other regions.
